key_ideas: Founding text of mathematical voting theory: group majorities can be cyclic (the Condorcet paradox); the candidate who beats each other in pairwise majority should win.
No rule turning individual rankings into a social ranking satisfies Pareto, independence of irrelevant alternatives and non-dictatorship when there are three options or more.
Every non-dictatorial voting scheme with at least three possible outcomes can be manipulated: some voter gains by misreporting.
Proves the same strategy-proofness impossibility independently and shows its correspondence with Arrow's theorem.
With single-peaked preferences, the median voter's favourite beats every other option in pairwise majority: majority rule is then transitive.
Between two options, simple majority is the only rule that is anonymous, neutral and positively responsive.
Probability of the Condorcet paradox for three options under random preferences, about 8.8% for a large electorate.
Proposes the ranking that minimises the total number of pairwise disagreements with the voters' rankings (the Kemeny rule).
A majority-rule equilibrium in several dimensions needs very restrictive symmetry of preferences, so it generally fails to exist.
When no majority equilibrium exists in two or more dimensions, majority cycles span the whole space: an agenda setter can reach almost any outcome.
The core of a simple game is non-empty for all preference profiles if and only if there are fewer options than the Nakamura number; with a veto player, the core is never empty.
A q-majority rule has an undominated option for every profile in d dimensions if and only if q exceeds d/(d+1) (with T options, (T-1)/T). Basis of Proposition 8.
With a concave density of ideal points, a 64% majority (1 - 1/e) has an unbeatable proposal and no cycles.
The optimal voting quota minimises the sum of external costs, which fall as the quota rises towards unanimity, and decision costs, which rise with it.
Simple majority maximises a voter's expected agreement with collective decisions when the voter does not know their future preferences.
An agenda setter making take-it-or-leave-it proposals extracts more the worse the reversion point (status quo) is for the voters.
Every Condorcet-consistent rule violates participation (the no-show paradox) when there are four options or more.
A computable solution for the probability of the voting paradox under random preferences.
Monograph on the probability of Condorcet's paradox under various probability models of preferences.
Behavioural social choice: majority cycles are rare in real election data; the impartial culture overstates them.
A ranking model in which rankings are more likely the closer they are to a central ranking; a standard generator of structured preferences (not yet cited in the note).
Aggregation of preferences with a variable electorate; origin of the Smith set, the smallest set of options that beat all outside options.
Axiomatic characterisation of Borda's rule.
Classification and properties of Condorcet social choice functions.
Kemeny's rule is the unique ranking rule that is neutral, consistent and Condorcet-consistent.
Reinterprets Condorcet's own theory: his maximum-likelihood approach leads to the Kemeny ranking.
Measures of voter choice behind the minimax (Simpson-Kramer) rule: elect the option whose worst pairwise defeat is smallest.
Defines independence of clones and proposes Ranked Pairs, which satisfies it; plurality suffers vote splitting and Borda teaming.
A tie-breaking refinement makes Ranked Pairs completely independent of clones.
The Schulze (beatpath) method: Condorcet- and Smith-consistent, independent of clones, monotonic, reversal-symmetric, computable in O(m^3).
Split Cycle discards the weakest majority in every cycle: independent of clones, immune to spoilers, satisfies positive and negative involvement; often not single-winner.
Stable Voting, a single-winner refinement of Split Cycle.
Many voting rules elect the winner of the nearest consensus profile under some distance: choosing a rule is choosing what counts as consensus.
Probabilistic social choice based on pairwise majorities, the origin of maximal lotteries.
The bipartisan set: the support of the optimal mixed strategy of the majority tournament game, a Condorcet-consistent tournament solution.
Maximal lotteries are characterised by population-consistency and composition-consistency.
Proposes approval voting: voters approve any number of candidates and the most approved wins; analyses its strategic and normative properties.
Handbook on approval voting: theory, experiments and practice.
Majority Judgment: voters grade every candidate on a common scale, and candidates are ranked by their median grade.
Book-length theory of Majority Judgment: measuring, ranking and electing with grades.
Critical evaluation of Majority Judgment: the paradoxes and properties it violates.
Systematic review of the paradoxes affecting single-winner procedures: non-monotonicity, no-show, clone effects, and others.
Spatial models reproduce observed ballots better than the impartial culture, under which cycles are overstated.
Experts in voting theory voted on voting rules at a 2010 workshop: plurality came last.
Compares multi-candidate rules by simulation and defines social utility efficiency, the efficiency measure used in Section 7.
54 rules compared on survey data and simulations: IRV and Condorcet-IRV hybrids are the least manipulable; most rules have similar utilitarian efficiency.
Book on collective decisions and voting, including evidence on Condorcet winners in real elections and the design of Ranked Pairs.
PrefLib, a public library of real preference data for testing voting rules.
Computing the winner of Kemeny's and Dodgson's rules is NP-hard.
Computational complexity as a barrier to manipulation: for some rules, finding a successful manipulation is NP-hard.
Survey: worst-case hardness of manipulation does not protect typical elections.
Handbook of computational social choice: axioms, algorithms and complexity of voting rules, tournament solutions and manipulation.
Voting by veto: each member proposes one option, the status quo is added, and members strike options in turn; it always decides and no member gets their worst outcome.
The proportional veto principle: a coalition can veto a number of options proportional to its size, and the resulting core is never empty.
Neutral rules implementable in strong equilibrium need veto power distributed roughly in proportion to coalition size; voting by successive veto is an example.
Textbook on the strategy of social choice: manipulation, implementation and veto procedures.
Computes the proportional veto core in polynomial time and gives an anonymous, neutral rule that selects from it; a pessimist can manipulate the core in polynomial time.
Families of rules that always select from the veto core, examined against monotonicity, participation and independence of unanimous losers.
Measures the majority power and veto power of common rules: more majority power usually comes with more veto power; proportional veto, Borda and Black's rule favour minorities.
Fallback bargaining: parties descend their rankings in lockstep until an option is common to all; Pareto-optimal and maximises the worst rank; with an impasse line it can end without agreement.
The majoritarian compromise (descend until a majority agrees) is majoritarian-optimal and implementable in subgame-perfect equilibrium.
Proposes the majoritarian compromise as an electoral mechanism and discusses its design.
Compares compromise rules between two parties, such as shortlisting, and their strategic properties.
Shortlisting procedures to balance two parties' power when appointing an officer.
Veto-rank, a solution to the two-person implementation problem that selects compromise outcomes.
Defines compromise as an equal-loss principle and shows that several 'compromise' rules fail to select one once the result is known.
Alternating vetoes give non-cooperative foundations to the area-monotonic bargaining solution.
Majority rule with veto power aggregates information better than unanimity and dominates it in large committees: separate blocking from approving.
Laboratory evidence that majority with veto outperforms unanimity.
More veto players, and more distance between them, reduce the ability to change the status quo (policy stability).
Book-length veto-player theory across political institutions.
Legislative bargaining with random recognition: proposers capture a large share, depending on the voting rule and the members' patience.
With an endogenous status quo, collective choice becomes inert and inefficient: today's decision constrains tomorrow's.
Dynamic bargaining with a veto player, theory and experiments: the vetoer's power grows over rounds.
Experiment: veto players capture more of the surplus, and committees with vetoers take longer to agree.
In unanimity bargaining, the possibility of commitment creates conflict and inefficient delay.
Majority against unanimity with private information: unanimity brings more delay and costlier bargaining.
With a veto player and incomplete information, the optimal mechanism delegates an interval of options to the vetoer.
Veto rights deter policy experimentation under redistributive constraints: a case against vetoes.
Stability of policies in dynamic bargaining with veto players.
Bargaining in standing committees whose default option is the previous decision: dynamics and inefficiency.
Sequential voting procedures are open to agenda manipulation.
When the agenda is formed endogenously, the proposal maker holds substantial power.
Propose or vote: a one-round procedure in which each member either proposes or votes; it reaches the Condorcet winner under symmetric single-peaked preferences.
Voting with random proposers: two rounds may suffice to reach the Condorcet winner.
New forms of democratic procedure designed to improve collective decisions.
Unanimity against majority when proposers have incomplete information: the comparison depends on what proposers know.
When members are responsible for their votes (expressive payoffs), unanimity can improve communication in committees.
Experiments on communication before voting in bargaining games with unanimity.
Laboratory committees in which anyone can veto (unanimity rule).
Under tacit consent, effective veto power is much smaller than formal power: social pressure and a fallback majority vote constrain objections.
The liberum veto (unanimity) of the Polish-Lithuanian Sejm, linked to religious fractionalisation, paralysed decision-making.
When voting is costly, the optimal procedure is sequential, with a threshold that falls over rounds.
IETF rough consensus: lack of disagreement matters more than agreement; consensus is reached when all objections are addressed, not necessarily accommodated.
Debian general resolutions: ranked ballots including 'None of the above' as default, quorum and supermajority against the default, Schulze count.
EU Council qualified majority: 55% of members and 65% of the population; a blocking minority needs at least four members.
Storable votes: voters can save votes across decisions and spend them where they care most.
SAT solving gives the optimal voter bound (12) for the no-show paradox of Condorcet-consistent rules.
